picked.t: Vietnam seeks broader visa exemptions for high-potential tourism markets
picked.body: Under a draft resolution that the government submitted to the National Assembly on Saturday, visa policies will also be designed with flexibility tailored to specific markets, with priority given to high-spending, long-stay tourists, repeat travelers and those combining leisure trips with business, conferences or seminars. The draft covers seven key policy groups, including investment incentives, business support, nighttime economy development, human resource, visa policies and tourism infrastructure. Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism Lam Thi Phuong Thanh said the proposed policies aim to remove existing bottlenecks and attract investment, positioning tourism as a key economic sector and a driver of the country's goal of achieving double-digit economic growth. The National Assembly is expected to vote on adopting the resolution on Nov. 21. Vietnam received 19.5 million international visitors in the first 10 months of 2026, a 13.8% increase from a year earlier, as it eyes 25 million foreign arrivals by the end of this year. China, South Korea and Russia are the country's biggest source of inbound tourists. Vietnam currently grants visa exemptions to citizens of 39 countries, allowing stays from 14 to 90 days.

picked.t: Vietnam eyes 24/7 entertainment zones, tax holidays for billion-dollar tourism projects
picked.body: The draft resolution on special mechanisms and policies for tourism development, submitted to lawmakers on Saturday, sets out seven groups of policies, ranging from investment incentives and business support to the night-time economy, workforce training and infrastructure. Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism Lam Thi Phuong Thanh said the policies aim to clear bottlenecks, draw investment and make tourism a key economic sector that helps drive the country's double-digit growth target. Under the draft, incentives would be tiered by investment capital, number of jobs and type of project, and concentrated in Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang as well as tourism centers, national tourism areas and areas with national tourism potential. High-quality tourism projects with total investment of at least VND3 trillion, at least VND1.5 trillion of it for tourism components, and creating at least 1,000 jobs could receive infrastructure support inside and outside the project site and priority in promotion. Domestic investors in this tier could also rent unused state-owned houses and land. Catalyst tourism projects worth at least VND10 trillion, with at least VND5 trillion for tourism components and at least 1,500 jobs, would be eligible on a five-year pilot basis for a preferential corporate income tax rate as low as 10%, half Vietnam's standard 20% rate, plus land rent exemptions or reductions set by the government. The highest incentives would go to strategic projects with total investment of at least VND30 trillion, including at least VND15 trillion for tourism components, and at least 2,000 jobs. They could operate for up to 70 years, be exempt from corporate income tax for up to four years and have their tax cut by up to 50% for no more than nine years after that. None of the three tiers would cover casino, prize-winning electronic gaming, betting or real estate components, Thanh said, as incentives would apply only to tourism activities. The government also proposed a pilot cut of up to 30% in land rent for landscaped areas, green space, water surfaces and shared spaces not used directly for business at resort hotels rated four stars or above, provided they are in tourism centers or national tourism areas and have a gross building density below 25%. Businesses opening new air routes for tourism could receive support, as could travel firms and accommodation providers that sign long-term contracts to buy products certified under the One Commune One Product (OCOP) program, which promotes local specialties. For new business models, the draft offers incentives for complexes combining tourism, entertainment, culture and sports; for tourism combined with healthcare and medical treatment; and for activities involving local communities. Businesses would also be encouraged to use artificial intelligence, virtual reality, augmented reality and other new technologies to develop products and improve the visitor experience. Some large-scale performing arts complexes, concert halls, festival streets, integrated entertainment zones and night-time economy activities would be allowed to operate 24/7 under a pilot of up to five years. They could follow shortened administrative procedures and obtain a one-time license for large international art programs and events held regularly, instead of reapplying for each edition. The state budget would fund training for high-quality tourism workers in management, foreign languages, vocational skills, digital transformation, digital content creation and innovation, as well as for local workers in community tourism areas. Budget funding would be prioritized for essential infrastructure and multimodal transport links from international gateways to growth poles, key tourism centers and national tourism areas. The state would also support the national tourism promotion program and help localities develop distinctive products and community tourism in ethnic minority, mountainous, border, island and disadvantaged areas. Reviewing the draft, Nguyen Dac Vinh, chairman of the National Assembly's Committee for Culture and Society, said the committee supported special policies focused on projects able to lead and spread tourism growth in key areas. But the committee found the incentives for strategic catalyst projects had been set at a very high level without an assessment of the benefits they would bring, and asked that they be weighed carefully. It also asked the government to explain how the minimum capital thresholds and the share of capital reserved for tourism were set, and whether the criteria for classifying projects were feasible. The committee said casino, prize-winning electronic gaming, betting and real estate components must stay outside the incentives, and that support should be tied to project results so the policy cannot be used to develop businesses outside priority sectors. picked.t: Asia's 'best' island Phu Quoc tops winter holiday wishlists of South Korean families
picked.body: The island moved up four places from last year to lead the ranking, ahead of Fukuoka and Osaka in Japan. The ranking was based on accommodation searches made by South Korean travelers accompanied by at least one child for stays between November 2026 and January 2027. The data was released by Agoda on Oct. 30. Two other Vietnamese destinations, Nha Trang and Da Nang, also made the top 10, ranking fourth and sixth. The list also included Tokyo, Okinawa, and Sapporo in Japan, Cebu in the Philippines, and Chiang Mai in Thailand. Agoda said Phu Quoc’s appeal to families was supported by the start of its dry season in November, enabling outdoor activities. Visitors can island-hop, snorkel, parasail, and visit night markets, theme parks, and safaris. Earlier this year, Phu Quoc was named Asia’s Best Island for a second consecutive year at Condé Nast Traveler’s 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards. Phu Quoc welcomed 2.1 million international tourists in the first 10 months of 2026, up 59% year-on-year, while total arrivals exceeded 9.2 million, according to local authorities.

picked.t: 5 Vietnamese restaurants named among Asia-Pacific's 100 best by Tatler
picked.body: Anan Saigon, Upstairs Tasting Room, Nephele, and CieL Dining in Ho Chi Minh City joined Hanoi's Gia on the list that was unveiled in Shanghai last month. The selection brings together restaurants offering different interpretations of Vietnamese cooking and menus drawing on European and other Asian influences. Set within a market, Anan Saigon offers chef Peter Cuong Franklin's creative takes on familiar Vietnamese dishes, from tacos inspired by banh xeo , the country's crispy savory pancakes, to fish sauce ice cream. Vietnamese flavors also shape the 12-course tasting menu at Upstairs Tasting Room, led by chef Hiep Truong. His dishes range from wagyu beef salad with small eggplants and herbs to charcoal-grilled duck inspired by a traditional Hue recipe from central Vietnam. At Nephele, a renovated historic building provides the setting for a single dinner tasting menu with Vietnamese influences. The meal unfolds across the property, beginning on the ground floor and continuing upstairs in the main dining room before ending with small sweets at the bar as vinyl records play, according to the Michelin Guide. In Thao Dien area, home to HCMC's largest expat community, CieL Dining brings European and Asian influences together in a minimalist dining room with an open kitchen. Brittany oysters are paired with sparkling wine and green apple, while herbs grown at the restaurant find their way into its dishes. Hanoi representative Gia explores Vietnamese culinary traditions through a seasonal tasting menu centered on local ingredients. Its setting on Van Mieu Street echoes the connection to heritage, with interiors inspired by the nearby Temple of Literature. Four of the five, Anan Saigon, Upstairs, CieL, and Gia, have one Michelin star in the 2026 selection. Upstairs earned its first star this year. Tatler covers dining, travel, fashion, and culture, and its annual Tatler Best awards recognize restaurants, hotels, and bars across the Asia-Pacific. Winners are selected through editorial nominations and evaluations by hospitality professionals, critics, journalists, and experienced travelers.

picked.t: Former Scottish judo star rebuilds life 10 years after near-fatal Vietnam accident
picked.body: The accident happened on May 10, 2016, after Inglis finished a volunteer English teaching session in the former Ha Long City, northern Vietnam's Quang Ninh Province, The Press and Journal reported. She was sitting sideways on a motorbike while wearing a long skirt when its hem became caught in the wheel, throwing her onto the road. The impact fractured her skull and broke her neck in two places, leaving her in a coma. Doctors estimated her chance of survival at just 1%. Before the accident, Inglis was an accomplished judoka who had won a silver medal at the 2014 Commonwealth Games. She had arrived in Vietnam in January 2016 to teach English to disadvantaged children. After receiving emergency treatment and spending several weeks in hospital in Vietnam, she was flown back to Edinburgh in June 2016. Her repatriation was made possible by a community fundraising campaign that raised more than US$400,000 for her medical expenses. When she regained consciousness after a month-long coma, she heard medical machines beeping and saw her parents nearby. Confused, she wondered why they had come to Vietnam, unaware that she had already returned to Scotland. She also did not know that surgeons had removed part of her skull during treatment. Her rehabilitation lasted years. Once an elite athlete, Inglis struggled to walk, frequently forgot words and needed help with basic personal care. During one physiotherapy session, she was asked to climb stairs. Having previously trained by running up steps at Murrayfield Stadium, she expected the exercise to be easy. Instead, she nearly fell backward after taking just a few steps. She later moved back in with her parents so they could monitor her seizures. Although her speech and communication gradually recovered, she had to abandon her competitive judo career. Doctors warned that another blow to the head could be life-threatening. She attempted to resume training, but pain around the titanium plate protecting her skull made professional competition impossible. "It took me a long time to get over it, and at one point I didn't even want to be near judo anymore," she said. With her Olympic ambitions over, Inglis turned to teaching. Despite doctors warning that office-based work could be difficult because of her brain injury, she completed her university degree during the Covid-19 pandemic. In 2022, she married construction engineer Ally Morrison and completed her teacher training. Three years later, the couple welcomed a son, and Inglis secured a job as a primary school teacher. She remains connected to judo by refereeing competitions and hopes to become a coach when her son is older. Looking back on the past decade, Inglis sees her recovery as a second chance at life. She often introduces herself as the luckiest person when meeting someone new. "I am lucky because I've practically lived two lives and pursued two different careers that I truly love," she said.

picked.t: China buys 96% of Vietnam’s durian exports
picked.body: Durian shipments fetched more than US$3.45 billion during the period, a 25% year-on-year jump, according to preliminary statistics from the customs department. Mainland China accounted for nearly $3.3 billion, a 27.6% increase and a market share that went up from 93.6% last year. Papua New Guinea was a distant second at $37.7 million, followed by Hong Kong at $36.7 million, and the U.S. at nearly $20.5 million. Dang Phuc Nguyen, secretary general of the Vietnam Fruit and Vegetable Association, said mainland China was a particularly important market because consumers there favored fresh durian whereas many other markets primarily consumed frozen and processed products. But this concentration would leave durian exports vulnerable if China tightened quality requirements or simply reduced imports. Durian was a high-value fruit but ripened quickly and was difficult to store for extended periods without deep freezing. When shipments were unable to clear customs on schedule, the risk of backlogs at packing facilities in the Mekong Delta and Central Highlands increased, putting pressure on sellers to offload at steep discounts. Markets such as the U.S., EU, Japan, South Korea, and Australia had potential but could not absorb large volumes of fresh durian diverted at short notice. These markets mainly consumed frozen products or cater to Asian customers, making them unable to replace China in terms of sales volume. The risks also extended to growers’ bargaining power. During the peak harvest season, when supply surged and sales depended largely on customs clearance of shipments to China, farmers often found themselves in a weak position. If exports stalled, traders could reduce purchases or force prices down, while growers lacked cold storage facilities to hold their produce until the market recovered. Durian exports had grown more slowly than expected this year and selling prices were lower during the peak season, as growing areas in the Mekong Delta faced problems with high cadmium levels, while erratic rains and sunny weather in the Central Highlands affected quality and output. To reduce the risks of dependence, the industry’s immediate priority should be to maintain stable access to China by controlling quality at growing areas , particularly cadmium and pesticide residues, and ensuring traceability. Local authorities needed to expand testing capacity and strengthen oversight of growing-area codes and packing facilities to limit shipments that fail to meet standards. Over the longer term, businesses needed to invest in cold storage, freezing, and further processing, including frozen durian flesh, ice cream, cakes, and durian powder, to extend shelf life and facilitate transport to distant markets. Companies should also expand their presence in markets covered by trade agreements such as the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and the EU-Vietnam Free Trade Agreement, targeting premium segments, supermarket chains, and Asian customers in the U.S., Japan, and E.U. while meeting GlobalG.A.P. or organic standards. The industry also needed stronger cooperation between the government, scientists, businesses, and farmers. Companies should sign long-term purchase agreements with cooperatives, coordinate harvest plans and invest in cold storage and logistics in growing areas to secure supply and reduce pressure to sell quickly during the peak season or when exports were disrupted. Vietnam’s durian exports could rise by 20% this year to $4.5-4.7 billion.

picked.t: Students recount moments of panic as fire engulfs Hanoi school, killing one
picked.body: Around noon on Thursday, she was dropped off by her mother at the school’s temporary campus on Hoang Tich Tri Street in Kim Lien Ward. She arrived early to prepare for the literature exam in the afternoon. The school has nearly 3,000 students in 61 classes. As its permanent campus on Luong Dinh Cua Street is being rebuilt, it moved at the start of the 2026-27 school year to a temporary location on Hoang Tich Tri Street, 500 m away. After studying for about 15 minutes, Vy heard an explosion and smelled something burning. Before she could process what was happening, she heard the shouted warnings. She quickly opened her backpack, swept all the books and belongings from her desk into it, and dragged a friend out, running out of the classroom. Outside, she saw thick black smoke billowing from a classroom in the sixth-grade building. It gradually spread over the parking area, just several dozen meters from where she was standing. Students poured out of their classrooms into the yard and headed toward the main gate and the yard of another primary school next door as their teachers shouted instructions. Vy said: "We were pushing and squeezing past one another, shouting ‘hurry up’ as we ran. Many students even fell." She went straight to a friend's house near the school and informed her mother. Many of her friends had been playing in the schoolyard when they heard the fire warning and fled. The entire evacuation lasted about five minutes. Although she made it home safely, Vy said she was still shaken by the incident, adding that she had never experienced such panic before. Kim Lien students attend classes in two shifts, grades eight and nine in the morning and grades six and seven in the afternoon. The fire broke out at around 12:15 p.m. just after the morning session ended at 11:45 a.m., though many students stayed back for other activities. The afternoon-shift students were preparing for classes, which start at 12:30 p.m. Manh was among those who had stayed behind after the morning session. He was chatting with friends when he heard a loud explosion. Some students rushed out, shouting there was a fire. He ran back to his classroom to look for his friends and saw black embers floating outside the door. After quickly brushing the particles off his trousers, he urged his classmates to "run outside quickly." Meanwhile, a parent on Hoang Tich Tri Street said the smoke spread quickly, billowing through gaps in the metal sheets in the roof and filling the area with a strong burning smell. She also heard several popping sounds, similar to explosions from the outdoor units of air conditioners. As thick black smoke rose high into the air, spreading to neighboring Phuong Mai Kindergarten and Hoang Tich Tri Street, parents rushed to Kim Lien Secondary School's temporary campus after hearing about the fire to look for their children. Linh, who has a child in seventh grade there, was working two kilometers away when she heard about the fire and rushed to the scene. Though she did not have much trouble finding her child, since the two have a fixed meeting point for pickups, she said the chaotic scene left her frightened and trembling in the legs and almost in tears. "I only breathed a sigh of relief when I saw my child was safe. Both the children and their parents were extremely stressed. Many students said they had only managed to run out without taking anything with them." Seven fire engines, a command vehicle, and more than 60 firefighters were dispatched to tackle the blaze. Firefighters arrived at the scene within four minutes after the blaze broke out, and determined that people were trapped inside. They began spraying water, searching for those trapped, and preventing the fire from spreading. By 12:40 p.m., the fire was largely under control and was completely extinguished by 1 p.m. Desks, chairs, and equipment in the sixth-grade building were charred. The metal-sheet roof and surrounding walls were warped and turned silver. Dozens of outdoor air-conditioning units remained on the roof, covered in soot. Behind the classroom building, dozens of bicycles were reduced to bare frames. Two neighboring classroom blocks also sustained partial fire damage. During search and rescue operations, police found one person dead and handed the body over to medical authorities. The victim was later identified as a sixth-grade male student . The boy and his older sister both attended Kim Lien Secondary School, about 7 km from their home. His sister is in ninth grade and attends morning classes, while he attended afternoon classes. Their father drove him to and from school every day. The cause of the fire is still under investigation. Hanoi Vice Chairman Do Anh Tuan has ordered relevant authorities to address the aftermath and investigate the cause. picked.t: American-style dining in Ho Chi Minh City skyscraper
picked.body: Opened in late September, the restaurant is the first Asian location for the American steakhouse chain founded in 1990. Spanning around 500 m2 and with 120 covers, the restaurant operates as an authentic American steakhouse. Stanley Ko, president of Ko Hospitality Group, the operator of The Capital Grille in Vietnam, says Ho Chi Minh City was selected as the brand's first regional destination due to its dynamic economy, sizable business community, and diners who are open to western foods. The restaurant serves an à la carte menu featuring appetizers, soups, salads, beef, seafood, side dishes, and desserts, with portion sizes adjusted to suit local dining habits. Beef takes center stage with diverse options in cuts, portion weights, levels of doneness, and sauces. The eatery exclusively serves imported USDA Prime beef, the highest grade in the U.S. Department of Agriculture quality system, known for abundant marbling that enhances tenderness and flavor when cooked. The restaurant's signature offering is its dry-aged beef (pictured). Aged for 18 to 24 days in a temperature- and humidity-controlled room, the process reduces moisture content, tenderizes muscle fibers, and deepens the natural flavor profile. A 680-gram dry-aged steak portion, good for three to four diners, costs VND3.2 million (US$124). The menu also highlights recognizable American classics. The caviar dip, priced at VND1.9 million, offers a twist on standard "chips and dip" by pairing crispy potato chips with caviar and caramelized onion dip. The lobster bisque, priced at VND450,000 per portion, is a steakhouse staple rooted in French tradition. It features a velvety crustacean-based broth combined with cream and seasonings, served alongside Spanish sherry, an aged fortified wine that elevates the soup's aroma and depth of flavor. Meanwhile, the lobster mac and cheese, priced at VND800,000, features macaroni tossed in cheese sauce and mixed with lobster meat. This is a variation of "mac and cheese," an iconic dish introduced to formal American banquets by President Thomas Jefferson in the early 19th century before becoming a household staple following Kraft's boxed release in 1937. Shannon Dean and Michael Zack, tourists from the U.S. visiting HCMC in late October, dined at the restaurant to enjoy some familiar flavors after trying local dishes. Having visited The Capital Grille in Las Vegas before, both said the food and decor closely matched U.S. standards, creating a sense of familiarity. For them, the highlight was pairing a familiar meal with panoramic city views at prices similar to the brand's U.S. locations. Local diners have also shared their impressions. A family of four from Ho Chi Minh City visited the restaurant to experience high-floor dining in the city center. Ordering a 10-course meal across appetizers, soups, steaks, seafood, and desserts, they observed that the dishes featured large portions, rich and creamy flavors, and fewer green vegetable options, with some items feeling slightly dry for Vietnamese palates. Their meal cost nearly VND13 million, which was similar to prices at other high-end steakhouses in the city. A staff member sets the table before welcoming dinner guests to the restaurant, which charges a 5% service charge. The restaurant is open from 11:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. and from 5:30 p.m. to 9:30 p.m. Guests are required to make reservations in advance and can use a dedicated elevator and private entrance (pictured).

picked.t: New pedestrian overpasses set to transform downtown Ho Chi Minh City's riverfront
picked.body: Vehicles travel along Ton Duc Thang Street near Me Linh Square. Photo by Nguyen The Duong One pedestrian bridge will be built at the intersection of Ton Duc Thang and Nguyen Hue streets, directly in front of the Majestic Saigon Hotel. The second bridge will be located at the intersection of Thai Van Lung and Ton Duc Thang streets, in front of The Landmark building, nearly 1km away. Between these two upcoming bridges lies the Bach Dang Wharf Park. Stretching along the Saigon River, the park already attracts large numbers of residents and tourists for recreation and sightseeing every day. With a the nipa palm-shaped pedestrian bridge across the river expected to be completed next February, officially connecting the city center with the Thu Thiem New Urban Area, visitor numbers in this area are expected to surge. Construction barriers now line both sides of Ton Duc Thang Street as workers lay the foundations for the pedestrian bridge extending from Nguyen Hue Street. Great Wealth Trading and Services Co. Ltd. is developing the project under a build-transfer (BT) contract that requires no financial contribution from the city. The two overpasses carry an estimated cost of VND88 billion (US$3.3 million). The developer proposed the infrastructure update and is fully financing the construction through corporate capital and other legitimate funding sources.
